models_evaluated: Netherton et al. vertebral body autocontouring tool (X-Net localization, deep learning contouring, random forest QA model)

links.outcome: Performance across two external sites versus original site (identification rate, QA accuracy)
links.effect: Off-the-shelf IR reduced by 11% and QA accuracy by 14% at dataset A; IR reduced 2% and QA accuracy 7% at dataset B versus baseline.
links.quote: Compared to the performance metrics obtained on MDA data, IR was reduced by 11 % and QA accuracy was reduced by 14 % across all vertebral bodies when used on dataset A ( Table 1 ).

links.outcome: Performance degradation when applied to external populations and scanner settings differing from development data
links.effect: Performance metrics decreased on average for all spinal regions on external data; dataset A had higher metastatic burden and thicker slices (3 mm vs optimal 2.5 mm).
links.quote: When the tool was used off-of-the shelf, performance metrics were decreased on average for all spinal regions for external data when compared to baseline data.

links.outcome: Identification rate before vs after local post-processing adjustment
links.effect: Post-processing adaptation increased identification rate by 4% on average (p<0.01) for dataset A and 4% (p=0.01) for dataset B; QA performance improved for A only (p=0.02) in results.
links.quote: This technique improved IR on dataset A by 4 % (p < 0.01) on average and also 4 % on dataset B (p = 0.01) on average across all regions ( Table 1 ).

links.outcome: Local performance on external institution data versus baseline
links.effect: Off-the-shelf accurate identification 83% (A) and 92% (B); identification, contour acceptability and QA accuracy reduced versus original testing dataset.
links.quote: Identification rate, contour acceptability rate and QA accuracy were reduced on both datasets compared to accuracies and rates measured on the model's orginal testing dataset.

unlisted_practices: Adding a secondary independent model-based automated QA check to flag contouring and labeling errors

models_evaluated: Netherton et al. vertebral body autocontouring and QA tool
adapted post-processing version of the vertebral body autocontouring and QA tool

links.effect: Dataset A: IR reduced by 11 % and QA accuracy by 14 % versus MDA data.
links.quote: Compared to the performance metrics obtained on MDA data, IR was reduced by 11 % and QA accuracy was reduced by 14 % across all vertebral bodies when used on dataset A ( Table 1 ).

links.effect: Dataset B: IR reduced by 2 % and QA accuracy by 7 % versus baseline data.
links.quote: Compared to the performance metrics obtained on baseline data, IR was reduced by 2 % and QA accuracy was reduced by 7 % across all vertebral bodies when used on dataset B ( Table 1 ).

links.effect: Post-processing improved IR by 4 % on dataset A (p < 0.01) and 4 % on dataset B (p = 0.01).
links.quote: This technique improved IR on dataset A by 4 % (p < 0.01) on average and also 4 % on dataset B (p = 0.01) on average across all regions ( Table 1 ).

links.effect: Off-shelf all-region IR/CR/QA accuracy: A 83 %/77 %/71 %; B 92 %/84 %/76 %; F1 A 0.58, B 0.54.
links.quote: All performance metrics, except for F1-score, were higher for dataset B than those from the dataset A when the tool was used off-the-shelf ( Table 1 ).

links.outcome: atypical anatomy and poor CT quality
links.effect: Struggled with several patients with extensive metastases and two patients with very poor CT scan image quality.
links.quote: The tool also struggled to identify certain vertebral levels with several of the patients from both institutions due to extensive metastases throughout the spine ( Fig. 3 A) as well as two patients with very poor CT scan image quality.

links.quote: Identification rate, contour acceptability rate and QA accuracy were reduced on both datasets compared to accuracies and rates measured on the model's orginal testing dataset.
